results.title: The Power of Regional Expertise in Comparative Politics
results.content: One crucial aspect that can significantly enhance the quality and accuracy of comparative politics research is regional expertise. In this article, we will explore the benefits of regional expertise in comparative politics, discuss strategies for integrating it into research, and examine case studies that demonstrate its successful application. Incorporating regional expertise into comparative politics research can have several benefits, including: ### Enhancing Research Accuracy and Nuance through Regional Context Regional expertise can provide researchers with a nuanced understanding of the regional context in which political phenomena occur. * Identify region-specific factors that influence political outcomes * Avoid cultural and historical biases that can lead to misinterpretation of data * Develop more accurate and context-specific research questions and hypotheses For instance, when studying the impact of democratization on economic growth, regional expertise can help researchers understand how different regional factors, such as the legacy of colonialism or the presence of natural resources, can shape the relationship between democracy and economic development. * Identify common patterns and trends across regions * Develop more nuanced and context-specific theories and frameworks * Compare and contrast the effectiveness of different policy interventions across regions The following diagram illustrates the benefits of regional expertise in comparative politics: Integrating Regional Expertise into Research To effectively integrate regional expertise into comparative politics research, researchers can employ several strategies, including: ### Strategies for Incorporating Regional Expertise into Research Design 1. Case Studies in Regional Expertise Several case studies demonstrate the successful application of regional expertise in comparative politics research. The following table summarizes the benefits and strategies for integrating regional expertise into comparative politics research: Regional expertise is a crucial component of comparative politics research, enabling researchers to develop more nuanced and accurate understandings of political phenomena across different regions. ### Q: Why is regional expertise important in comparative politics research? A: Regional expertise is important in comparative politics research because it can enhance research accuracy and nuance, inform policy-making, and facilitate cross-regional comparisons and analysis.

results.title: [2009.14304] Cross-lingual Alignment Methods for Multilingual BERT: A Comparative Study
results.content: [Submitted on 29 Sep 2020]. # Title:Cross-lingual Alignment Methods for Multilingual BERT: A Comparative Study. View a PDF of the paper titled Cross-lingual Alignment Methods for Multilingual BERT: A Comparative Study, by Saurabh Kulshreshtha and 2 other authors. > Abstract:Multilingual BERT (mBERT) has shown reasonable capability for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer when fine-tuned on downstream tasks. Since mBERT is not pre-trained with explicit cross-lingual supervision, transfer performance can further be improved by aligning mBERT with cross-lingual signal. Prior work proposes several approaches to align contextualised embeddings. In this paper we analyse how different forms of cross-lingual supervision and various alignment methods influence the transfer capability of mBERT in zero-shot setting. fine-tuning based alignment methods. We evaluate the performance of different alignment methodologies across eight languages on two tasks: Name Entity Recognition and Semantic Slot Filling. In addition, we propose a novel normalisation method which consistently improves the performance of rotation-based alignment including a notable 3% F1 improvement for distant and typologically dissimilar languages. Importantly we identify the biases of the alignment methods to the type of task and proximity to the transfer language. We also find that supervision from parallel corpus is generally superior to dictionary alignments. **[v1]** Tue, 29 Sep 2020 20:56:57 UTC (164 KB). ## Access Paper:. results.title: Evaluation of Sampling and Cross-Validation Tuning Strategies for Regional-Scale Machine Learning Classification
results.content: Although many studies have compared machine learning classification methods, sample selection methods for acquiring training and validation data for machine learning, and cross-validation techniques for tuning classifier parameters are rarely investigated, particularly on large, high spatial resolution datasets. This work examines sample selection and cross-validation parameter tuning on regional-scale land cover classifications using HR remotely sensed data. * Which training sample selection method results in the highest classification accuracy for a supervised support vector machine (SVM) classification of a regional-scale HR remotely sensed dataset? A total of 36 individual classifications were conducted, each using a different combination of sample and validation methods: 3 categories of approaches at different spatial scales and sample sizes (small subset, small regional, and large regional) × 4 sample selection methods (simple random, proportional stratified random, disproportional stratified random, and deliberative) × 3 cross-validation tuning methods (k-fold, leave-one-out, and Monte Carlo) = 36 classifications. Within each spatial scale and sample size (i.e., subset, small regional, and large regional), the disproportional stratified random (DSTR) samples consistently resulted in the highest overall accuracy although it is notable that variations between the performance of the classifications trained using the different statistical-based sampling methods were small, less than 2%. There was no consistent pattern for the overall accuracy of the classifications trained from the small subset samples and tuned using the three cross-validation methods (k-fold, Monte Carlo, and leave-one-out). The cross-validation tuning methods using the small regional SR, PSTR, and DSTR training data applied to the SVM classification all showed high values for overall accuracy (Figure 8b) and inconsistent results for the different tuning methods, similar to the results of the small subset training data. This investigation explored the effects sample acquisition method, sample geographic distribution, and cross-validation tuning methods in regional-scale land-cover classifications of HR remotely sensed data. The relative accuracy of classifications produced with k-fold (k = 10), leave-one-out, and Monte Carlo cross-validation tuning methods when trained with the small subset, small regional, and large regional SR, PSTR, and DSTR data sets were not consistent. Regarding deliberative sampling methods, in both the small subset and large regional classifications, leave-one-out cross-validation tuning was more effective in increasing classifier performance when compared to the k-fold and Monte Carlo tuning.
